Following the claim, the CAC summoned representatives from the seven companies, but the probe zeroed in on DeepSeek and Moonshot, the people added.
DeepSeek and Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Seeking Alpha.
DeepSeek is set to brief the United Nations Security Council this week on risks posed by AI, Reuters reported.

This is not the first time that U.S. AI labs have accused Chinese AI labs of using distillation, a practice that has brought ire from U.S. politicians. Anthropic issued a letter to White House officials and U.S. Senators in June, claiming that Alibaba had used distillation to improve the performance of its models. Anthropic said it had evidence showing that operators linked to Alibaba's Qwen AI lab conducted 28.8M exchanges with Claude through about 25,000 fraudulent accounts.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump Administration would be entitled to sanction open-weight models from China if evidence of distillation from American models is verified. “We are finding watermarks of our U.S. large language models on many of the Chinese models, and that's unacceptable,” Bessent said at the time. “We're going to be looking at that in the coming days or weeks.”
Moonshot AI, which is backed by Alibaba, released Kimi K3 in July, which it said is the world's largest open-weight AI model. Alibaba released a preview of its flagship Qwen 3.8 Max in July.

U.S. intelligence agencies, including the FBI, issued a statement earlier this month to American AI labs to safeguard their IP after accusing major Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, of systematically harvesting proprietary data from American models.

The topic is of heightened interest as President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet this week in Washington. Among the topics to be discussed between the two world leaders is the role of artificial intelligence and its usage.
